question: With reference to the MGNREGA scheme, how many days of guaranteed wage employment is provided to rural unskilled labour?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 100.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment in a financial year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. (अकुशल श्रम — unskilled labour)

• The Act came into force on 2 February 2006, first launched in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh, covering 200 districts; it was extended to the whole country by 2008.

• It is implemented by the Ministry of Rural Development; if employment is not provided within 15 days of application, the applicant is entitled to an unemployment allowance.

• At least one-third of the beneficiaries must be women, and works must be within 5 km of the applicant's residence.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• 150 days — the enhanced entitlement given to households in drought/natural-calamity notified areas (an extra 50 days over the basic 100).

• 120 days / 90 days — not linked to MGNREGA's statutory guarantee; these are distractors.

• The scheme was renamed from NREGA to MGNREGA on 2 October 2009.

NOTE

• MGNREGA is the world's largest rights-based social security and public-works programme, backed by a legal guarantee.

• Related schemes: PMAY-G (housing), DDU-GKY (rural skill training), NRLM/Aajeevika (self-help groups), all under the Ministry of Rural Development.

question: In 1600, the East India company acquired a charter from _______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Queen Elizabeth I.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The English East India Company was granted a royal charter by Queen Elizabeth I on 31 December 1600, giving it a monopoly of English trade with the East. (राजाज्ञा/अधिकार-पत्र — charter)

• The charter was originally for 15 years; the Company's first factory in India was set up at Surat in 1613, after Captain Hawkins and later Sir Thomas Roe (envoy of James I) visited Jahangir's court.

• The Company's first voyage to the East was led by Captain James Lancaster.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• King Edward VI (1547–1553) — son of Henry VIII; ruled long before the Company existed.

• King Henry IV — an English king of the early 15th century (1399–1413), unrelated to the Company.

• Queen Victoria — under her, the Government of India Act 1858 transferred power from the Company to the British Crown; she was proclaimed Empress of India in 1877.

NOTE

• Other European companies: Portuguese (Vasco da Gama, Calicut, 1498), Dutch (1602), Danish (1616), French (1664, Colbert under Louis XIV).

• Key English factories: Surat (1613), Madras/Fort St. George (1639), Bombay (1668), Calcutta/Fort William (1690).

question: The Council of States shall consist of _______ members to be nominated by the President.
solution_text:
The correct answer is twelve.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under Article 80 of the Constitution, the Council of States (Rajya Sabha) consists of 12 members nominated by the President plus not more than 238 representatives of the States and Union Territories — a maximum strength of 250. (राज्य सभा — Council of States)

• The 12 nominated members are persons having special knowledge or practical experience in literature, science, art and social service.

• Present actual strength of the Rajya Sabha is 245 (233 elected + 12 nominated).

• Members are elected by the elected MLAs of State Assemblies through proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• The Lok Sabha (House of the People) — Article 81; maximum strength 550 (530 States + 20 UTs). The provision for 2 nominated Anglo-Indians was abolished by the 104th Amendment Act, 2019.

• The Rajya Sabha is a permanent house — it is never dissolved; one-third of its members retire every 2 years, each member serving 6 years.

• Minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership is 30 years (Lok Sabha: 25 years).

NOTE

• The Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 64) and is not a member of the House.

• Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha can retain a Money Bill for a maximum of 14 days.

question: Plant cell has a big central ______ unlike a number of small ______ in animal cells.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vacuole, vacuoles.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A mature plant cell has one large central vacuole that may occupy up to 90% of the cell volume, while animal cells have several small vacuoles. (रसधानी — vacuole)

• The vacuole is bounded by a membrane called the tonoplast and is filled with cell sap containing water, sugars, amino acids and pigments.

• Functions: it provides turgidity and rigidity to the plant cell, stores nutrients, and holds waste products.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Cell wall — present only in plant cells (made of cellulose); animal cells have no cell wall, so the second blank could not be "cell walls".

• Tissue — a group of cells, not a cell organelle, so it cannot fit "a big central ______".

• Cell membrane (plasma membrane) — present in both plant and animal cells, but only one per cell, not "a number of small" ones.

NOTE

• Organelles found only in plant cells: cell wall, plastids (chloroplast), large central vacuole.

• Organelles found only in animal cells: centrosome/centrioles and lysosomes (abundant); lysosomes are called "suicidal bags" of the cell.

• Mitochondrion is the "powerhouse" of the cell; ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.

question: Among the following, which of these are an example of capital receipt?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Borrowings and loan recovery.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Capital receipts are receipts that either create a liability (e.g. borrowings) or reduce an asset (e.g. recovery of loans, disinvestment proceeds). (पूंजीगत प्राप्तियां — capital receipts)

• Revenue receipts, in contrast, neither create a liability nor reduce assets — e.g. taxes, interest, rent, dividend, commission, fees and fines.

• Borrowing creates a debt liability for the government, and loan recovery reduces the financial asset held by it — so both are capital receipts.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Rent and commission received — regular, recurring income; these are revenue receipts.

• Sale of goods and rent — sale of goods is ordinary business income, hence revenue, not capital (sale of a fixed asset would be capital).

• Commission and dividend received — both are revenue receipts as they arise from routine operations/investments.

NOTE

• Fiscal deficit = Total expenditure − Total receipts excluding borrowings; it is financed mainly by borrowings.

• Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure − Revenue receipts; Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit − Interest payments.

• Disinvestment (sale of government shareholding in PSUs) is a capital receipt because it reduces government assets.

question: Which kathak dancer was awarded with Padma Shri and Sangeet Natak Akademi Award?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sitara Devi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sitara Devi (1920–2014) was a legendary Kathak dancer, singer and actress, popularly called "Nritya Samragyi" (Empress of Dance) — a title given to her by Rabindranath Tagore. (कथक — a North Indian classical dance)

• She received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1969 and the Padma Shri in 1973; she also received the Kalidas Samman (1995).

• She was born in Kolkata to a Banarasi Brahmin family and learnt Kathak from her father Sukhdev Maharaj.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Hema Malini — an actress and trained Bharatanatyam dancer, awarded the Padma Shri (2000); she is not primarily a Kathak exponent.

• Kaushalya Reddy — a Kuchipudi dancer, wife of Kuchipudi exponent Raja Reddy.

• Sridevi — a film actress (Padma Shri 2013), not a classical dancer by profession.

NOTE

• Famous Kathak exponents: Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi, Shambhu Maharaj, Lachhu Maharaj, Gopi Krishna, Damayanti Joshi.

• Gharanas of Kathak: Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras (and Raigarh).

• The Sangeet Natak Akademi, India's national academy for music, dance and drama, was set up in 1953 with headquarters in New Delhi.

question: "Playing It My Way" is an autobiography of ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sachin Tendulkar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Playing It My Way" (2014) is the autobiography of Sachin Tendulkar, co-written with Boria Majumdar. (आत्मकथा — autobiography)

• Sachin, the "Master Blaster", is the only cricketer with 100 international centuries and over 34,000 international runs; he played 200 Test matches, a world record.

• He received the Arjuna Award (1994), Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna (1997–98), Padma Shri (1999), Padma Vibhushan (2008) and the Bharat Ratna (2014).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• M S Dhoni — his life is portrayed in the biopic *M.S. Dhoni: The Untold Story*; the book "The Dhoni Touch" is by Bharat Sundaresan.

• Rahul Dravid — biography "Rahul Dravid: Timeless Steel"; he is nicknamed "The Wall".

• Yuvraj Singh — autobiography "The Test of My Life", about his fight against cancer after the 2011 World Cup (he was Player of the Tournament).

NOTE

• Other sports autobiographies: "Unbreakable" — Mary Kom, "Ace Against Odds" — Sania Mirza, "A Shot at History" — Abhinav Bindra, "Straight from the Heart" — Kapil Dev, "Sunny Days" — Sunil Gavaskar.

question: According to Census 2011, which among the following has the minimum population density?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Arunachal Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• As per Census 2011, Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest population density in India at about 17 persons per sq km. (जनसंख्या घनत्व — population density)

• Population density = Total population ÷ Total area (persons per sq km). India's overall density in 2011 was 382 persons per sq km.

• Arunachal Pradesh has a very large hilly, forested area with a small population (about 13.8 lakh), which keeps its density lowest.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Chandigarh (UT) — density about 9,258 persons/sq km, one of the highest in the country.

• Andhra Pradesh — about 308 persons/sq km (undivided state figure was 308).

• Sikkim — about 86 persons/sq km, the lowest among states after Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram.

NOTE

• Census 2011 highs and lows: Highest density state — Bihar (1,106); Highest UT — Delhi (11,320); Lowest density UT — Andaman & Nicobar Islands (46).

• Most populous state — Uttar Pradesh; least populous state — Sikkim; largest state by area — Rajasthan.

• Census 2011 was the 15th Census of India and the 7th after Independence; its motto was "Our Census, Our Future".

question: India is set to surpass _______ to become the world's most populous country by 2023, says a report by the United Nations.
solution_text:
The correct answer is China.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The United Nations World Population Prospects 2022 report projected that India would overtake China as the world's most populous country in 2023. (जनसंख्या — population)

• The UNFPA State of World Population Report 2023 confirmed it: India's population reached about 142.86 crore against China's 142.57 crore.

• The world's population crossed the 8 billion mark on 15 November 2022, according to the same UN projections.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• United States of America — the third most populous country (about 34 crore), far behind India and China.

• Indonesia — the fourth most populous country and the largest Muslim-majority nation.

• Pakistan — the fifth most populous country; it was earlier part of undivided India.

NOTE

• World Population Day is observed on 11 July every year.

• UNFPA (United Nations Population Fund) publishes the annual State of World Population report; UNDESA publishes World Population Prospects.

• India's decadal growth rate (2001–2011) was 17.7%; the sex ratio in Census 2011 was 943 females per 1,000 males.

question: A temporary alliance of groups or parties is called a _______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Coalition.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A coalition is a temporary alliance of distinct parties or groups formed to achieve a common goal — most often to form a government when no single party wins a majority. (गठबंधन — coalition)

• India's first coalition government at the Centre was the Janata Party government (1977) under Morarji Desai.

• Major coalitions in Indian politics include the NDA (formed 1998) and the UPA (formed 2004).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Veto — the power to reject a decision or law; the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (USA, UK, Russia, China, France) hold veto power. The Indian President has absolute, suspensive and pocket veto.

• Constituency — a specific territorial area whose voters elect a representative to a legislature.

• Federalism — a system dividing powers between a central government and constituent states; India follows a quasi-federal system with a strong Centre.

NOTE

• The Indian Constitution's federal features come mainly from Canada; the Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists.

• The Anti-Defection Law is contained in the Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.

question: Which of the following Indian singers has won a Grammy award?
solution_text:
The correct answer is A R Rahman.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A. R. Rahman won two Grammy Awards in 2010 for *Slumdog Millionaire* — Best Compilation Soundtrack for Visual Media and Best Song Written for Visual Media ("Jai Ho"). (ग्रैमी पुरस्कार — Grammy Award)

• In the same year he also won two Academy Awards (Oscars) — Best Original Score and Best Original Song — plus a Golden Globe and a BAFTA.

• Known as the "Mozart of Madras", he received the Padma Shri (2000) and Padma Bhushan (2010); his debut film score was Roja (1992).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Kumar Sanu — Bollywood playback singer, Padma Shri (2009); holds a Guinness record for recording the most songs in a day, but no Grammy.

• Arijit Singh — a leading contemporary playback singer; he has won Filmfare and National Film Awards, not a Grammy.

• Mohammed Rafi — legendary playback singer, Padma Shri (1967) and six Filmfare Awards; he died in 1980.

NOTE

• Other Indians/Indian-origin Grammy winners: Pandit Ravi Shankar, Zakir Hussain, Vishwa Mohan Bhatt, Ricky Kej, Falguni Shah (Falu).

• The Grammy Awards are presented by the Recording Academy of the USA; the first ceremony was held in 1959.

question: Annie Besant laid the foundation of the Central Hindu College in _______ in 1898 where both Hindu religion and Western scientific subjects were taught.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Benaras.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Annie Besant founded the Central Hindu College at Benaras (Varanasi) in 1898, where both Hindu religion and Western scientific subjects were taught. (काशी/बनारस — Benaras)

• This college later became the nucleus of the Banaras Hindu University (BHU), established in 1916 by Madan Mohan Malaviya.

• Annie Besant, an Irish-origin theosophist, started the Home Rule League in 1916 (Madras) and became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress at the Calcutta session, 1917.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Pune — associated with the Deccan Education Society (1884) and Fergusson College (1885) of Tilak, Agarkar and Chiplunkar; also the Servants of India Society (1905) of Gopal Krishna Gokhale.

• Chennai (Madras) — Annie Besant's Theosophical Society headquarters are at Adyar, Chennai, and she published the newspaper New India from there.

• Kolkata (Calcutta) — home of the Hindu College (1817) founded with Raja Rammohan Roy's support, later Presidency College.

NOTE

• The Home Rule Movement had two leagues — Bal Gangadhar Tilak's (April 1916, Belgaum/Poona) and Annie Besant's (September 1916, Madras).

• The Theosophical Society was founded in 1875 in New York by Madame Blavatsky and Colonel Olcott; its Indian headquarters shifted to Adyar in 1882.

question: Article 356 and 360 in the Indian constitution are the articles based on _______ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is emergency provisions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Articles 352 to 360 in Part XVIII of the Constitution deal with Emergency Provisions. (आपातकालीन उपबंध — emergency provisions)

• Article 356 — President's Rule / State Emergency, imposed on the failure of constitutional machinery in a State.

• Article 360 — Financial Emergency, which can be proclaimed if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened; it has never been imposed in India.

• Article 352 — National Emergency, on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion; declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Regional languages — dealt with in Part XVII (Articles 343–351); the Eighth Schedule currently lists 22 languages.

• Amendment of the Constitution — Article 368 (Part XX).

• Elections — Part XV (Articles 324–329); Article 324 establishes the Election Commission of India.

NOTE

• The emergency provisions are borrowed from the Government of India Act, 1935 (and the German Weimar Constitution for suspension of Fundamental Rights).

• The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion" in Article 352 and made Article 20 and 21 non-suspendable during an Emergency.

question: Sachin Tendulkar received the “Bharat Ratna Award” in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2014.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sachin Tendulkar was conferred the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, on 4 February 2014 by President Pranab Mukherjee. (भारत रत्न — Bharat Ratna)

• He is the first sportsperson and, at the age of 40, the youngest recipient of the Bharat Ratna.

• Scientist C. N. R. Rao received the award along with him in the same ceremony.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• 2013 — the year in which the award was announced (16 November 2013), the day Sachin played his final Test match at the Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai.

• 2011 — the year India won the ICC Cricket World Cup, Sachin's sixth World Cup.

• 2012 — the year Sachin was nominated to the Rajya Sabha and scored his 100th international century (16 March 2012, vs Bangladesh at Mirpur).

NOTE

• The Bharat Ratna was instituted in 1954; the first recipients were C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan and C. V. Raman.

• Foreign-born recipients: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1987) and Nelson Mandela (1990).

• The order of civilian awards is Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri; a maximum of three Bharat Ratnas may be given in a year.

question: Sultan Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraja III in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1192.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraja III (Prithviraj Chauhan) in the Second Battle of Tarain in 1192, a turning point that opened North India to Turkish rule. (तराइन का द्वितीय युद्ध — Second Battle of Tarain)

• Tarain (Taraori) lies near Thanesar in present-day Haryana.

• After the victory, Ghori left India under his slave general Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who founded the Slave (Mamluk) Dynasty in 1206, the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• 1191 — the First Battle of Tarain, in which Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad Ghori.

• 1211 — the year Iltutmish ascended the throne of Delhi.

• 1195 — around the time of the Battle of Chandawar (1194), where Ghori defeated Jaichandra of Kannauj (Gahadavala dynasty).

NOTE

• Muhammad Ghori's first Indian victory was over Prithviraj's ally-less forces at Tarain II; he was assassinated in 1206.

• Prithviraj Raso, a Braj epic by Chand Bardai, narrates Prithviraj Chauhan's life.

• Earlier invader: Mahmud of Ghazni raided India 17 times (1000–1027), including the sack of the Somnath temple (1025).

question: How many white squares are there on a chessboard?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 32.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A standard chessboard is an 8 × 8 grid = 64 squares, coloured alternately, so there are 32 white (light) squares and 32 black (dark) squares. (शतरंज — chess)

• Each player begins with 16 pieces: 1 king, 1 queen, 2 rooks, 2 bishops, 2 knights and 8 pawns — a total of 32 pieces on the board.

• Chess is believed to have originated in India as Chaturanga during the Gupta period.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• 64 — the total number of squares (both colours) on a chessboard, not just the white ones.

• 204 — the total number of squares of all sizes (1×1 to 8×8) that can be counted on a chessboard: 64+49+36+25+16+9+4+1 = 204.

• 22 — not related to any chessboard count; a pure distractor.

NOTE

• Viswanathan Anand was India's first Grandmaster (1988) and a five-time World Chess Champion.

• The international chess body is FIDE (Fédération Internationale des Échecs), founded in 1924, headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland.

• International Chess Day is celebrated on 20 July; the 44th Chess Olympiad (2022) was hosted at Mahabalipuram, Chennai.

question: Which vitamin is soluble in water?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vitamin-C.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a water-soluble vitamin; so is the entire vitamin B-complex. Excess water-soluble vitamins are excreted in urine and are not stored in the body. (जल में घुलनशील — water-soluble)

• Deficiency of vitamin C causes scurvy (bleeding gums, weakness); rich sources are amla, guava, citrus fruits, tomato and green chillies.

• Vitamin C is destroyed by heat/cooking, which is why fruits rich in it are best eaten raw.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Vitamin-A (Retinol) — fat-soluble; deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia.

• Vitamin-D (Calciferol) — fat-soluble; the "sunshine vitamin"; deficiency causes rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

• Vitamin-E (Tocopherol) — fat-soluble antioxidant; deficiency causes sterility/reproductive problems.

NOTE

• Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K (remember "ADEK"); Water-soluble: B-complex and C.

• Vitamin K (Phylloquinone) helps in blood clotting; Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamin) deficiency causes pernicious anaemia; Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency causes beri-beri.

question: The breaking up of the rocks on the earth’s surface is called as ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is weathering.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Weathering is the breaking up and decay of rocks in situ (in their own place) on the earth's surface by physical, chemical and biological agents. (अपक्षय — weathering)

• Types: physical/mechanical (frost action, temperature change, exfoliation), chemical (oxidation, carbonation, hydration, solution) and biological (roots, burrowing animals, humans).

• Weathering is the first step in soil formation and, unlike erosion, involves no transport of material.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Stacking — a stack is a coastal landform: an isolated pillar of rock left standing in the sea after a sea arch collapses.

• Meandering — the winding, S-shaped course of a river in its middle/lower course; a cut-off meander forms an ox-bow lake.

• Sorting — the grading/separation of sediment particles by size during deposition.

NOTE

• Erosion = wearing away plus transport of material by water, wind, ice or waves; mass wasting = downslope movement under gravity.

• Fluvial (river) landforms: V-shaped valley, gorge, waterfall, meander, ox-bow lake, flood plain, delta.

• Glacial landforms: cirque, arete, horn, U-shaped valley, moraine, drumlin.

question: The Elephanta Caves are located in which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Maharashtra.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Elephanta Caves are on Elephanta (Gharapuri) Island in Mumbai Harbour, Maharashtra, about 10 km from Mumbai. (एलिफेंटा गुफाएँ — Elephanta Caves)

• They are rock-cut caves dedicated mainly to Lord Shiva, famous for the colossal Trimurti (Maheshmurti) sculpture; they were built roughly between the 5th and 8th centuries CE.

• They were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987; the name "Elephanta" was given by the Portuguese after a stone elephant statue found there.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Gujarat — UNESCO sites include Champaner-Pavagadh, Rani ki Vav (Patan), Historic City of Ahmedabad and Dholavira.

• Rajasthan — Hill Forts of Rajasthan, Jantar Mantar (Jaipur), Keoladeo National Park and the walled city of Jaipur.

• Karnataka — Hampi, Pattadakal and the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas (Belur, Halebid, Somanathapura).

NOTE

• Other UNESCO sites in Maharashtra: Ajanta Caves (Buddhist paintings), Ellora Caves (Buddhist, Hindu and Jain — includes the Kailasa temple), Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus and the Victorian Gothic & Art Deco Ensembles of Mumbai.

• India's first UNESCO World Heritage Sites (1983) were Ajanta Caves, Ellora Caves, Agra Fort and Taj Mahal.

question: Kuchipudi is a classical dance of which state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Andhra Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kuchipudi is the classical dance form of Andhra Pradesh, named after the village Kuchelapuram (Kuchipudi) in Krishna district. (कुचिपुड़ी — Kuchipudi)

• It was systematised in the 17th century by Siddhendra Yogi, whose famous dance-drama is "Bhama Kalapam".

• Its signature items are the Tarangam, performed balancing a pot of water on the head while dancing on the rim of a brass plate.

• Noted exponents: Vempati Chinna Satyam, Raja and Radha Reddy, Yamini Krishnamurthy, Swapnasundari.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Tamil Nadu — Bharatanatyam, the oldest classical dance, earlier called *Sadir*; exponents include Rukmini Devi Arundale and Balasaraswati.

• Kerala — Kathakali (male, elaborate make-up) and Mohiniyattam (the lone female "dance of the enchantress").

• Bihar — has no recognised classical dance; its folk forms include Jat-Jatin, Bidesia and Jhijhian.

NOTE

• The eight classical dances recognised by the Sangeet Natak Akademi: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (Uttar Pradesh), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• All classical dances derive from the Natya Shastra of Bharata Muni.

question: The Himalayan Mountain range was formed by the collision of ________ .
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indian Plate and Eurasian Plate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate, which began about 50 million years ago and still continues. (हिमालय — the Himalayas)

• This is a convergent boundary of the continental–continental type, which produces fold mountains rather than volcanoes.

• The sea that lay between the two plates was the Tethys Sea; its sediments were folded up to form the Himalayas — which is why marine fossils are found high in the range.

• The Himalayas are the youngest fold mountains in the world and are still rising by a few centimetres a year, making the region seismically active.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Collision of the African and Eurasian plates is associated with the Alps and the Atlas mountains, not the Himalayas.

• The Australian Plate collision zone lies to the far south-east of India and formed features around Indonesia/New Guinea.

• The Indian Plate broke away from the ancient supercontinent Gondwana and drifted northwards.

NOTE

• The three parallel ranges of the Himalayas: Himadri (Greater Himalaya), Himachal (Lesser Himalaya) and Shiwaliks (Outer Himalaya).

• Mount Everest (8,848.86 m) is the highest peak in the world; Kangchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest peak in India (Sikkim).

question: The basic unit of speed of an object is ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is metre per second (m/s).

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Speed = Distance ÷ Time. In the SI system, distance is measured in metre (m) and time in second (s), so the SI (basic) unit of speed is metre per second (m/s). (चाल — speed)

• Speed is a scalar quantity (magnitude only), while velocity is a vector (magnitude with direction); both have the same unit m/s.

• Conversion: 1 km/h = 5/18 m/s and 1 m/s = 18/5 km/h.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• metre per km (m/km) — a ratio of two lengths, so it has no time dimension and cannot measure speed.

• metre per hour (m/h) and metre per minute — valid but non-SI ways of expressing speed; "m/m" is also an incorrect symbol.

• Commercial speeds are usually quoted in km/h, and marine/aviation speeds in knots (1 knot = 1.852 km/h).

NOTE

• The seven SI base units: metre (length), kilogram (mass), second (time), ampere (electric current), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), candela (luminous intensity).

• Derived units: acceleration — m/s², force — newton (N = kg·m/s²), work/energy — joule (J), power — watt (W), pressure — pascal (Pa).

• The speed of light in vacuum is about 3 × 10⁸ m/s; the speed of sound in air is about 343 m/s at 20 °C.

question: Kicheri is a harvest festival and involves ritual bathing, celebrated majorly in ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Uttar Pradesh.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Khichdi (Kicheri) is the harvest festival celebrated mainly in Uttar Pradesh, observed on Makar Sankranti (14/15 January) with ritual bathing in rivers and the offering of khichdi. (खिचड़ी — Khichdi festival)

• The famous Khichdi Mela is held at the Gorakhnath Temple, Gorakhpur, where devotees offer khichdi (rice and pulses) to Baba Gorakhnath.

• Makar Sankranti marks the sun's entry into the zodiac sign Makara (Capricorn) and the beginning of Uttarayan, the northward journey of the sun.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Madhya Pradesh — festivals include Bhagoria (a tribal festival of the Bhils/Bhilalas) and the Khajuraho Dance Festival.

• Haryana — celebrates Lohri, Baisakhi, Teej and Gugga Naumi.

• Gujarat — celebrates the same day as Uttarayan, famous for the International Kite Festival at Ahmedabad.

NOTE

• Harvest festivals of India: Pongal (Tamil Nadu), Makar Sankranti (North India), Lohri (Punjab), Bihu (Assam), Onam (Kerala), Baisakhi (Punjab), Nuakhai (Odisha), Wangala (Meghalaya).

• Other UP festivals: Kumbh/Magh Mela (Prayagraj), Dev Deepawali (Varanasi), Ram Navami (Ayodhya).

question: In which of the following methods of irrigation, the water falls drop by drop directly near the roots?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Drip system.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In drip irrigation (also called trickle irrigation), water falls drop by drop through a network of narrow pipes and emitters directly at the roots of plants. (टपक सिंचाई — drip irrigation)

• It is the most water-efficient method (efficiency up to 90%), minimising evaporation and runoff, and is ideal for arid regions and orchards/vegetable crops.

• Drip and sprinkler systems together are called micro-irrigation, promoted in India under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY) — "Per Drop More Crop".

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Manual irrigation — water applied by hand using cans or buckets; labour-intensive and suited only to small plots.

• Sprinkler system — water is sprayed into the air through nozzles and falls like rain; useful on sandy soil and uneven land, but loses water to evaporation.

• Lateral move irrigation — a moving-line sprinkler system in which pipes on wheels are shifted across the field; still a spray, not drop-by-drop.

NOTE

• Traditional irrigation methods: moat (pulley system), chain pump, dhekli, rahat (lever system).

• Modern methods: sprinkler, drip and centre-pivot irrigation.

• Sources of irrigation in India in order of area: tube wells/wells > canals > tanks.

question: Who among the following was defeated in the Battle of Kannauj in 1540?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Humayun.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• In the Battle of Kannauj (Bilgram), 17 May 1540, Sher Shah Suri decisively defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun, who then fled India and spent about 15 years in exile in Persia. (कन्नौज/बिलग्राम का युद्ध — Battle of Kannauj)

• A year earlier, Sher Shah had beaten Humayun in the Battle of Chausa (1539), after which he assumed the title "Sher Shah" and struck coins in his own name.

• The victory at Kannauj established the Sur Empire (1540–1555); Humayun regained Delhi only in 1555 after the Battle of Sirhind.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Akbar — born in 1542 at Amarkot, two years after this battle; he won the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).

• Hemu (Hemchandra Vikramaditya) — the Hindu ruler defeated and killed by Akbar's forces in the Second Battle of Panipat, 1556.

• Sher Shah — the victor, not the loser, of Kannauj; he died in 1545 at the siege of Kalinjar.

NOTE

• Sher Shah's reforms: the rupiya silver coin, the Grand Trunk Road (Sonargaon to Peshawar), sarais, an efficient dak (postal) system and land revenue reforms carried out by Todar Mal.

• Major Mughal-era battles: Panipat I (1526), Khanwa (1527), Ghaghra (1529), Chausa (1539), Kannauj (1540), Panipat II (1556), Haldighati (1576).
